quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on loom speed, efficiency, A- and B-grade, sizing and what counts as variable production cost.

questions.q: What does the rpm of a loom measure?
options: Picks inserted per minute at full speed
Revolutions of the warp beam per minute
questions.explain: One revolution of the loom's main shaft inserts one pick, so 800 rpm means 800 picks a minute when the loom is running.

questions.q: Loom efficiency of 90 % means…
options: the loom is actually inserting picks for 90 % of the available time
90 % of the warp ends are intact
the loom runs at 90 % of its rated rpm
questions.explain: Efficiency allows for stoppages for breaks, beam changes and so on; 800 × 0.9 = 720 effective picks per minute. Grade and rpm are separate ideas.

questions.q: B-grade fabric is fabric with faults that must be sold at a lower price.
questions.explain: The lecture deducts the B-grade share from production and then credits the lower B-grade price back as a small reduction in cost per A-grade metre.

questions.q: How is sizing cost charged in the lecture's sheet?
options: Per kg of sized warp in a metre of fabric
questions.explain: Sized warp per metre (0.124 kg) × sizing cost per kg (Rs 10) = Rs 1.24 per metre. Packing, by contrast, is charged per metre.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the variable production cost per metre in Lecture 19?
questions.explain: Depreciation is a fixed cost of the loom per day, compared with the contribution in Lecture 20. Yarn, sizing and packing vary with every metre made.

questions.q: The sheet assumes "all wastage in warping". What does this mean for the sizing calculation?
options: The warp weight used for sizing is the weight before wastage, since waste yarn never reaches the size box
Wastage is added to the sized warp
questions.explain: If the yarn lost as waste is lost at warping, it is never sized, so sizing is charged on the warp weight before wastage (with contraction) rather than on the grossed-up yarn weight.

questions.q: A-grade production per day is…
questions.explain: 480 yd × (1 − 0.01) = 475.2 yd of A-grade; the 4.8 yd of B-grade is sold separately at a lower price.

questions.q: The B-grade proceeds appear in the sheet as a negative cost, that is, a credit.
questions.explain: Row 18 shows (0.21): the B-grade metres are sold at Rs 21, and that income is credited against the cost of each A-grade metre.

questions.q: Which lecture supplies the yarn cost per metre used as row 10 of this sheet?
questions.explain: Lecture 18 computed the yarn cost of the 20×20/60×60, 63″ fabric as Rs 27.79 per metre; Lecture 19 adds the conversion costs to it.

questions.q: The production of a loom in inches per minute depends on…
options: rpm, efficiency and picks per inch
rpm, width and ends per inch
picks per inch and reed count
questions.explain: Inches per minute = rpm × efficiency ÷ picks per inch. Width does not affect length produced, and the warp has no part in it.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The loom production formula, the yard-to-metre conversion, and how each input moves the variable cost per metre.

questions.q: Production per minute (inches) equals…
questions.explain: 800 × 0.9 ÷ 60 = 12 inches per minute. Multiplying by picks per inch gives a nonsense figure of 43,200.

questions.q: Production per day in yards from inches per minute is…
questions.explain: A day has 1,440 minutes; 12 × 1,440 = 17,280 inches ÷ 36 = 480 yd. Using 60 minutes gives one hour's output only.

questions.q: If picks per inch rise from 60 to 80 at the same rpm and efficiency, the loom's daily production…
questions.explain: Length produced is inversely proportional to picks per inch: 60 ÷ 80 = 0.75, so 480 yd becomes 360 yd a day.

questions.q: Yards are converted to metres by…
questions.explain: 1 yd = 0.9144 m, so 475.2 yd × 0.9144 = 434.5 m. Multiplying by 1.0936 converts metres to yards, the opposite direction.

questions.q: Raising loom efficiency from 90 % to 95 % raises daily production by about 5.6 %.
questions.explain: Production is proportional to efficiency: 95 ÷ 90 = 1.056. 480 yd becomes about 507 yd a day.

questions.q: Sizing cost per metre equals…
options: sized warp per metre (kg) × sizing cost per kg
sizing cost per kg ÷ sized warp per metre
warp weight per yard × sizing cost per kg
questions.explain: 0.124 kg × Rs 10 = Rs 1.24 per metre. Using the weight per yard in lb without converting to kg per metre would mis-state it.

questions.q: The B-grade credit per A-grade metre is approximately…
questions.explain: Each A-grade metre carries about 1 % of a B-grade metre: Rs 21 × 0.01 ≈ Rs 0.21 credit (exactly 0.01 ÷ 0.99 × 21 = Rs 0.212).

questions.q: Total variable production cost per metre is…
questions.explain: Rs 27.79 + 1.24 + 0.50 − 0.21 = Rs 29.32 per metre. The B-grade proceeds are a credit and so are subtracted.

questions.q: If the sizing cost per kg doubles from Rs 10 to Rs 20, the variable cost per metre rises by…
questions.explain: Sizing cost per metre goes from Rs 1.24 to Rs 2.48, an increase of Rs 1.24. Sizing is a small share of the Rs 29.32 total.

questions.q: A higher B-grade percentage lowers the variable cost per A-grade metre because the B-grade credit grows.
questions.explain: The credit grows a little, but the yarn cost per A-grade metre (÷ (1 − B) in Lecture 18) and the lost A-grade production grow much more. B-grade always costs the mill money.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute loom output per minute and per day, A-grade metres, sized warp, sizing cost and the variable cost per metre.

questions.q: An air-jet loom runs at 800 rpm, 90 % efficiency, weaving 60 picks per inch. How many inches of fabric does it make per minute?
questions.explain: 800 × 0.9 = 720 picks per minute; ÷ 60 picks per inch = 12 inches per minute.

questions.q: A loom makes 12 inches per minute. How many yards does it make in a 24-hour day?
questions.explain: 12 × 1,440 minutes = 17,280 inches; ÷ 36 = 480 yd per day.

questions.q: Daily production is 480 yd and 1 % is B-grade. How many yards of A-grade are produced per day?
Convert 475.2 yd of A-grade fabric to metres (1 yd = 0.9144 m), to one decimal place.
questions.explain: 475.2 × 0.9144 = 434.5 m per loom per day.

questions.q: A metre of fabric contains 0.124 kg of sized warp and sizing costs Rs 10 per kg. What is the sizing cost per metre?
questions.explain: 0.124 × Rs 10 = Rs 1.24 per metre.

questions.q: Warp weight before wastage is 0.25 lb per yard. Convert to kg per metre (1 m = 1.0936 yd, 1 kg = 2.2046 lb), to three decimals.
questions.explain: 0.25 × 1.0936 = 0.2734 lb per metre; ÷ 2.2046 = 0.124 kg per metre, the sheet's sized warp figure.

questions.q: B-grade is 1 % of production and sells at Rs 21 per metre. Using credit = B-grade price × B-grade %, what is the credit per metre (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: Rs 21 × 0.01 = Rs 0.21 per metre, shown as (0.21) in the sheet.

questions.q: Yarn cost Rs 27.79, sizing Rs 1.24, packing Rs 0.50 and B-grade credit Rs 0.21 per metre. What is the total variable production cost per metre?
A loom at 600 rpm, 85 % efficiency, 48 picks per inch. Its daily production is…
questions.explain: 600 × 0.85 ÷ 48 = 10.625 in per minute; × 1,440 ÷ 36 = 425 yd. 510 yd ignores efficiency; 340 yd uses 60 picks.

questions.q: A loom makes 434.5 m of A-grade a day. If the mill has 120 such looms, how many metres of A-grade does it produce per day?

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Weaving-shed decisions: speed versus efficiency, the cost of B-grade, and checking a supplier's sizing quotation.

questions.q: A weaving manager can run the looms at 900 rpm with efficiency falling to 80 %, or stay at 800 rpm and 90 %. Which produces more?
options: 900 rpm at 80 %: 720 effective picks, the same as 800 at 90 %
They are equal, so choose 900 rpm
questions.explain: 900 × 0.8 = 720 = 800 × 0.9: identical output. But more stops at 900 rpm usually mean more faults and B-grade, so 800 rpm at 90 % is the safer choice.

questions.q: B-grade rises from 1 % to 4 % on a 480 yd per day loom. What is the main cost?
options: About 14 yd a day of A-grade are lost and sold at half price, and the yarn in them is still charged to A-grade
questions.explain: 480 × 0.03 = 14.4 yd a day drop from A-grade (Rs 42) to B-grade (Rs 21), about Rs 300 a day per loom, and the yarn cost per A-grade metre rises about 3 %.

questions.q: A size supplier offers a cheaper size at Rs 8 per kg instead of Rs 10, but warp breaks rise and efficiency drops from 90 % to 88 %. Per loom per day (434.5 m at 90 %), what is the net effect?
options: Saves about Rs 108 a day, worth it
Saves Rs 108 on sizing but loses about 10 m of A-grade production, costing more than it saves
questions.explain: Sizing saving: Rs 0.248 × 434.5 ≈ Rs 108. Production loss: 434.5 × (1 − 88 ÷ 90) ≈ 9.7 m; at a contribution of about Rs 11.7 per metre (Lecture 20) that is Rs 113 lost, before any extra B-grade. Roughly break-even at best.

questions.q: Packing cost per metre is unaffected by loom speed or efficiency.
questions.explain: Packing is charged per metre of fabric packed (Rs 0.50); how fast the loom made the metre does not matter.

questions.q: The mill switches the same fabric to a 400 rpm shuttle loom at 85 % efficiency. What happens to the per-metre variable production cost of Rs 29.32?
options: It is almost unchanged; only fixed cost per metre changes because the loom makes fewer metres a day
questions.explain: Yarn, sizing and packing per metre do not depend on loom speed. Output drops to about 5.7 in per minute (227 yd a day), so the loom's fixed daily cost is spread over fewer metres.

questions.q: An order for a 100-pick fabric is being planned on looms set for 60 picks. How many loom-days will 43,450 m of A-grade need, compared with about 100 loom-days at 60 picks?
questions.explain: Production falls in proportion to 60 ÷ 100, so loom-days rise by 100 ÷ 60: 100 × 1.667 ≈ 167 loom-days. Denser fabrics tie up looms for longer.

questions.q: The costing office is told the B-grade price has risen from Rs 21 to Rs 30 per metre. Effect on variable cost per A-grade metre?
questions.explain: The credit grows from 0.21 to 0.30 per metre (Rs 30 × 1 %), reducing cost by Rs 0.09. A 1 % share makes B-grade pricing a minor factor.

questions.q: A planner computes 480 yd per day and tells the customer 480 m will be delivered per loom per day. What is the error, roughly?
options: Over-promising by about 9 % plus the 1 % B-grade: about 434 m is realistic
No error, yards and metres are close enough
questions.explain: 480 yd is 439 m, and only 99 % of it is A-grade: 434.5 m. Promising 480 m overstates deliverable output by about 10 %.

questions.q: Because sizing is charged per kg of warp, a fabric with a heavier warp (more ends or coarser count) has a higher sizing cost per metre.
questions.explain: Sized warp per metre rises with ends and with coarser count, so at Rs 10 per kg the sizing cost per metre rises in proportion.

questions.q: Which of the following would NOT change the total variable production cost per metre?
options: Sizing cost per kg up Rs 2
Loom rpm up from 800 to 900 at the same efficiency
Packing cost up Rs 0.10 per metre
questions.explain: Speed changes how many metres are made a day, not what each metre costs in yarn, size and packing. It matters for fixed cost per metre and contribution per loom per day.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder, two-step problems linking loom production to cost per metre, and the mistakes that creep into weaving calculations.

questions.q: A loom runs at 750 rpm, 92 % efficiency, 72 picks per inch, with 2 % B-grade. How many metres of A-grade does it make per day (1 yd = 0.9144 m)? Answer to the nearest metre.

A metre of fabric has 0.162 kg of sized warp; sizing costs Rs 12 per kg, packing Rs 0.60 per metre, yarn Rs 31.40 per metre, and B-grade is 2 % selling at Rs 20 per metre (credit = price × B-grade %). Find the total variable production cost per metre, to the nearest paisa.

The lecture's loom makes 475.2 yd of A-grade and 4.8 yd of B-grade a day. A student credits the full B-grade sale (4.8 × Rs 21 ≈ Rs 101) against the day's cost and also divides by 480 yd to get a per-metre credit. What is wrong?
options: The credit should be spread over the A-grade metres sold, not over all 480 yd, and yards must be converted to metres
The B-grade price should be Rs 42
B-grade should not be credited at all
questions.explain: Costs are per A-grade metre: Rs 101 ÷ 434.5 m ≈ Rs 0.23 (the sheet shows 0.21 using the approximation B-grade price × B-grade %). Spreading over 480 yd mixes grades and units.

questions.q: Two looms: loom X at 800 rpm, 90 %, 60 picks per inch; loom Y at 1,000 rpm, 85 %, 60 picks per inch. How many more yards per day does Y make than X?
questions.explain: Y: 850 ÷ 60 = 14.17 in per min = 566.7 yd; X: 480 yd. Difference 86.7 yd per day, about 18 % more.

questions.q: At a fixed loom speed, a fabric with more picks per inch has a lower variable production cost per metre because the loom spends more time on it.
questions.explain: More picks mean more weft yarn per metre, so the yarn cost rises; loom time affects fixed cost per metre (Lecture 20), not the variable cost shown here.

questions.q: A sized warp weighs 0.124 kg per metre of fabric at 60 ends per inch. The same fabric is re-specified at 72 ends per inch with the same count. What is the new sized warp per metre, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Warp weight is proportional to ends: 0.124 × 72 ÷ 60 = 0.149 kg per metre, so sizing rises to about Rs 1.49 per metre.

questions.q: A mill reports loom production of 12 in per minute but only 400 yd a day instead of 480. Which explanation fits?
options: The loom works only 20 hours a day, not 24
questions.explain: 12 in per minute × 1,200 minutes ÷ 36 = 400 yd. The 1,440-minute day assumes three shifts; a mill running fewer hours should use its actual working minutes.

questions.q: Yarn cost per metre is Rs 27.79 and the other variable production costs net to Rs 1.53 per metre. What percentage of the Rs 29.32 variable production cost is yarn (to one decimal place)?
questions.explain: 27.79 ÷ 29.32 = 94.8 %. Yarn dominates, which is why Lecture 18's weight calculation deserves such care.

questions.q: If efficiency rises from 90 % to 95 %, which of the following is true about the sheet's figures?
options: Production per day and A-grade metres rise; variable cost per metre is unchanged
Production rises and variable cost per metre falls
Nothing changes because rpm is the same
questions.explain: Output goes from 434.5 m to about 458.6 m a day. Yarn, sizing and packing per metre are unaffected; the gain shows up as more contribution per loom per day in Lecture 20.

questions.q: A loom produces 434.5 m of A-grade per day at 800 rpm and 90 % efficiency. What production would it reach at 800 rpm and 95 % efficiency, to the nearest metre?
questions.explain: Production is proportional to efficiency: 434.5 × 95 ÷ 90 = 458.6 m per day.
